title: Beyond the Dashboard: Distinguishing Vanity Metrics from Actionable Insights
learningObjectives: Distinguish vanity metrics (look good but don't inform decisions) from actionable metrics
Design measurement systems that drive behavior change and learning
Practice saying no to meaningless measurement requests
Learn when detailed data collection creates burden without value

context.yourRole: Director of Digital Government Monitoring & Evaluation, Rwanda. You oversee performance measurement for all government digital services.
context.situation: Your team produces monthly dashboards with 147 indicators. Senior officials love the dashboards but services aren't improving. You suspect measuring the wrong things.
context.pressure: Ministers want to 'show progress' with impressive numbers. But you need metrics that actually help teams improve services.
context.reality: Most organizations measure what's easy, not what's useful. Good measurement requires discipline to focus on metrics that inform action.

rounds.situation:
Monthly performance review meeting. You present the dashboard:

**E-Services Dashboard (October 2025):**

📊 **Portal Traffic**
- Total visits: 1,247,583 (↑ 12% vs Sept)
- Page views: 4,892,441 (↑ 15% vs Sept)
- Unique visitors: 847,291 (↑ 9% vs Sept)
- Average session duration: 4.2 minutes (↑ 0.3 min)

📱 **Mobile App**
- Downloads: 89,431 (↑ 8% vs Sept)
- Monthly active users: 45,229 (↑ 6% vs Sept)
- App store rating: 4.1 stars (↔ same as Sept)

📄 **Services Performance**
- Total transactions: 234,677 (↑ 11% vs Sept)
- Business registration: 12,843 transactions (↑ 7%)
- Tax filing: 78,442 transactions (↑ 13%)
- Driving license renewal: 34,291 transactions (↑ 9%)
- [... 12 more services listed ...]

⚡ **System Performance**
- Average response time: 1.8 seconds (target: <2.0 sec) ✅
- Uptime: 99.4% (target: >99%) ✅
- Error rate: 0.7% (target: <1%) ✅

Permanent Secretary: "Excellent! Everything is green. Traffic up, transactions up, system performing well. Congratulations team."

Minister: "These numbers look impressive. We should share them with the press - 1.2 million visits, nearly 250,000 transactions. This shows our digital government is succeeding."

But you've been talking to service teams and hearing different story:

**Conversation with Tax Service Team (last week):**

Tax Officer: "We see the dashboard shows 78,000 tax filing transactions. But do you know how many of those actually succeeded? We get hundreds of calls daily from citizens saying they tried to file but got errors. The dashboard shows the transaction started, not that it completed successfully."

You: "How many actually succeed?"

Tax Officer: "We estimate maybe 60%. The other 40% abandon due to errors, confusion, or giving up and coming to the office instead."

**Conversation with Business Registration Team:**

Registration Officer: "The dashboard shows 12,800 business registrations. But that's registrations started, not completed. Many people start, get confused at Step 4 (beneficial ownership form), and abandon. We only complete about 70% of started applications. Plus, we're seeing same people register multiple times because they couldn't figure out if first attempt worked."

**Conversation with Citizen Call Center:**

Call Center Manager: "We receive 8,000 calls per month - 80% are people confused about digital services. Most common: 'I tried to use the website but it didn't work,' 'I don't know if my application went through,' 'The error message didn't tell me what to do.' But I don't see call center data in your dashboard at all."

**Conversation with Field Office Manager:**

Field Manager: "The dashboard shows online transactions are increasing. But so are in-person visits to our offices - up 15% this year. People try online, fail, then come to us. We're not reducing burden - we're just adding a failed digital channel before they use the in-person channel. We're making things worse."

You realize: **The dashboard shows activity, not success. It shows volume, not outcomes. It makes things look good without revealing problems.**

You return to the performance meeting:

You: "Minister, I appreciate the positive view. But I've been investigating behind these numbers. May I share some concerns?"

Minister (surprised): "Concerns? But everything is green."

You: "The metrics are green, but the reality is different. Let me give examples:

- We measure 'transactions started' but not 'transactions completed successfully.' 40% of tax filings fail.
- We measure 'business registrations' but not 'completion rate.' 30% abandon at Step 4.
- We measure 'portal visits' but not 'did they accomplish their goal.' Call center gets 8,000 frustrated calls monthly.
- We measure 'online transactions increasing' but in-person office visits are also up 15%. We're adding burden, not reducing it.

**Our dashboard measures activity. It doesn't measure whether we're helping citizens.**"

Permanent Secretary (uncomfortable): "But these are standard metrics. Every country measures portal visits and transaction volumes."

You: "Yes, and many countries have dashboards that look good while services remain frustrating. I think we're measuring vanity metrics - numbers that look impressive but don't tell us if we're succeeding."

Minister: "What do you propose?"

You: "I propose we redesign our measurement around actual outcomes: Did the citizen succeed? Did we save them time? Did we reduce frustration? These are harder to measure but actually useful."

Permanent Secretary (hesitant): "But if we measure completion rates and citizen satisfaction, the numbers might not look as good. That could reflect poorly on the program."

You: "Exactly. We might learn we're not doing as well as we thought. But that's the point - we can't improve if we don't measure honestly."
rounds.prompt: How do you distinguish vanity metrics from actionable metrics, and convince leadership to measure what matters?
evaluationCriteria: **Definition**: Do they clearly explain difference between vanity metrics (impressive but not actionable) vs actionable metrics (inform decisions)?
**Examples**: Do they provide concrete examples of each type?
**Behavioral Change**: Do they recognize that good metrics drive behavior change and learning?
**Uncomfortable Truth**: Do they acknowledge that actionable metrics might reveal problems, not just successes?
**User Outcomes**: Do they focus on end-user success rather than system activity?
**Political Navigation**: Do they understand why leadership prefers vanity metrics (look good) and how to shift mindset?
rounds.coachingNotes: Classic measurement problem in government: dashboards full of vanity metrics that look good but don't drive improvement. **Vanity metrics**: Portal visits, downloads, page views, transaction volumes (started). Look impressive, feel good, but don't tell you if you're helping citizens. **Actionable metrics**: Completion rate, time saved, citizen satisfaction, problem resolution rate, repeat visits (indicates failure). May reveal problems, but inform what to improve. The PS's concern ('numbers might not look as good') reveals the political challenge: leadership often wants measurement for external validation ('look how well we're doing') not for internal learning ('how can we improve'). You need to reframe: 'Do we want to look good or be good? Looking good with vanity metrics while citizens suffer is not success.' Frame actionable metrics as showing we're serious about real impact, not just theater.

rounds.situation:
You prepare a presentation for the Minister on measurement redesign:

**VANITY METRICS vs ACTIONABLE METRICS**

**Vanity Metric #1: Portal Visits**
- Current: 1.2M visits per month (↑ 12%)
- What it tells us: People are coming to website
- What it doesn't tell us: Did they find what they needed? Did they succeed?
- **Why it's vanity**: Visits can increase even as satisfaction decreases (people visiting repeatedly because they can't figure it out)

**Actionable Alternative: Task Success Rate**
- Measure: % of visits where user accomplished their goal
- How to measure: Exit surveys, completion tracking, call-back research
- What it drives: Focus on user experience, not just traffic
- Example: 'Only 45% of users accomplish their task on first visit'

---

**Vanity Metric #2: Transactions Started**
- Current: 234K transactions per month (↑ 11%)
- What it tells us: People are trying to use services
- What it doesn't tell us: Did they complete? Did they succeed?
- **Why it's vanity**: Transactions started can increase while completion rate decreases

**Actionable Alternative: Transaction Completion Rate**
- Measure: % of started transactions that complete successfully
- How to measure: Track from initiation to confirmation
- What it drives: Focus on fixing drop-off points, error handling
- Example: 'Tax filing completion rate is 60% - 40% abandon. Let's fix that.'

---

**Vanity Metric #3: Average Session Duration**
- Current: 4.2 minutes (↑ 0.3 min)
- What it tells us: Users spend time on site
- What it doesn't tell us: Are they productively completing tasks or confused and stuck?
- **Why it's vanity**: Longer sessions can mean confusion, not engagement

**Actionable Alternative: Time on Task vs Benchmark**
- Measure: How long does it take to complete specific tasks vs how long it should take?
- How to measure: Task-based timing with comparison to optimal path
- What it drives: Simplifying complex processes
- Example: 'Business registration takes average 47 minutes but should take 15 minutes. Where's the friction?'

---

**Vanity Metric #4: System Uptime**
- Current: 99.4% uptime ✅
- What it tells us: System is technically available
- What it doesn't tell us: Is it usable when it's up? Do errors occur within uptime?
- **Why it's vanity**: System can be 'up' but throwing errors, running slowly, or confusing users

**Actionable Alternative: Successful Transaction Rate**
- Measure: % of attempted transactions that complete without errors
- How to measure: Track end-to-end success, including user-facing errors
- What it drives: Focus on error handling, not just infrastructure
- Example: 'System is up 99.4% but only 73% of transactions succeed. Fix error handling.'

---

You present this to the Minister:

Minister (studying the comparison): "I see your point. Measuring 'visits' looks good but doesn't tell us if we're actually helping people. Measuring 'task success rate' might show we're only helping 45% of visitors - that's uncomfortable but useful."

You: "Exactly. Vanity metrics make us feel good. Actionable metrics make us better."

Permanent Secretary: "But if we report that only 45% of users succeed, or only 60% complete transactions, that could be used against us politically. Opposition might say 'government digital services are failing.'"

You: "True. But consider the alternative: we report vanity metrics that look good while citizens suffer frustration. Eventually, the gap between our metrics and their experience will undermine credibility. It's better to measure honestly and show improvement over time."

Minister (thinking): "What if we use both? Keep some vanity metrics for external reporting - showing progress, momentum. But add actionable metrics for internal management - showing what needs improvement. We need both audiences: public wants to see progress, our teams need to know where to improve."

You: "I can support that, with one condition: we don't let the vanity metrics drive internal decisions. It's fine to report 'visits increased 12%' externally, but internally we focus on 'task success rate improved from 45% to 52%.'"

Permanent Secretary: "So we have two dashboards? One for public, one for internal?"

You: "Not quite. One integrated dashboard, but we're clear about what metrics drive our decisions vs what metrics we report for transparency. Public can see both - we're not hiding anything. But we're explicit: 'Here's our activity metrics (vanity), here's our outcome metrics (actionable), and we manage based on outcomes.'"

Minister: "Okay, let's pilot this. Choose one service - let's say business registration. Implement this actionable measurement approach. Show me in 3 months if it makes a difference."

You: "Agreed."

**BUSINESS REGISTRATION - MEASUREMENT REDESIGN**

You work with the business registration team:

You: "Currently we measure 'registrations started' (12,843 last month). Let's add actionable metrics."

**New Metrics Added:**

1. **Completion Rate**
   - Started: 12,843
   - Completed: 8,991
   - **Completion Rate: 70%**
   - Insight: 30% abandon - why?

2. **Drop-off Analysis**
   - Step 1 (Business Details): 99% proceed
   - Step 2 (Owner Information): 95% proceed
   - Step 3 (Address Information): 91% proceed
   - **Step 4 (Beneficial Ownership): 67% proceed** ← Big drop!
   - Step 5 (Payment): 89% proceed
   - Step 6 (Confirmation): 97% proceed

3. **Time to Complete**
   - Average: 47 minutes
   - Optimal path: 15 minutes
   - **Excess time: 32 minutes** - where is friction?

4. **Error Rate**
   - Errors encountered: 68% of users
   - Most common error: "Beneficial ownership percentage must equal 100%"
   - Second most common: "Invalid tax identification number format"

5. **Support Requests**
   - Call center calls about business registration: 890/month
   - Most common question: "How do I fill out beneficial ownership form?"

6. **Offline Fallback Rate**
   - Users who start online but complete in-person: 18%
   - Reason (from survey): "Too confusing online, easier to ask staff"

Registration Officer: "Wow. This data tells a completely different story than 'registrations increasing.' We have a major problem at Step 4 (beneficial ownership), error messages are confusing, process takes 3x longer than it should, and 18% give up on digital channel and come to office anyway."

You: "Exactly. Now you know where to focus improvement efforts."

**IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS (based on actionable metrics):**

Team identifies fixes:

1. **Fix Step 4 (Beneficial Ownership)**
   - Add explanation video
   - Provide example scenarios
   - Add real-time validation ("Current total: 85%, need 15% more")
   - Simplify for single-owner businesses (auto-fill 100%)

2. **Improve Error Messages**
   - Change "Invalid tax identification number format" to "Tax ID should be 9 digits, format: XXX-XXX-XXX. Yours has 8 digits."
   - Add contextual help next to each error

3. **Add Save & Resume**
   - Allow users to save progress and return later (addresses 47-minute completion time)

4. **Proactive Support**
   - At Step 4, offer live chat option
   - Send email with instructions to users who abandon at Step 4

They implement these changes.
rounds.prompt: After implementing improvements based on actionable metrics, how do you know if the changes actually worked?
evaluationCriteria: **Before/After Comparison**: Do they measure same metrics before and after to see change?
**Leading vs Lagging**: Do they understand some metrics show impact quickly (leading) vs over time (lagging)?
**Segmentation**: Do they look at different user groups to see if improvements helped everyone equally?
**Unintended Consequences**: Do they check if improvements in one area caused problems elsewhere?
**Statistical Significance**: Do they understand need for enough data to distinguish real change from random variation?
**Continuous Learning**: Do they see measurement as ongoing learning loop, not one-time exercise?
rounds.coachingNotes: Implementing changes is only valuable if you verify they worked. Need structured before/after analysis: [1] **Baseline**: Establish metrics before change (70% completion, 47 min avg time, 890 support calls), [2] **After**: Measure same metrics after change, [3] **Comparison**: Calculate change and assess if meaningful. Also watch for: **Leading indicators** (show impact quickly - error rate, drop-off at Step 4) vs **Lagging indicators** (show impact over time - overall completion rate, support call reduction). **Segmentation** matters: improvements might help new users but not returning users, or vice versa. Check for **unintended consequences**: fixing Step 4 might create new problem at Step 5. **Statistical significance**: need enough data - don't conclude after 1 week. **Continuous loop**: measure → learn → improve → measure again. This is never finished.

rounds.situation:
**THREE MONTHS LATER - RESULTS**

**Business Registration Metrics - Before vs After:**

| Metric | Before (Baseline) | After (3 months) | Change |
|--------|------------------|------------------|--------|
| **Registrations Started** | 12,843 | 13,947 | +8.6% |
| **Completion Rate** | 70% | 84% | +14 pts |
| **Registrations Completed** | 8,991 | 11,715 | +30% |
| **Drop-off at Step 4** | 33% | 12% | -21 pts |
| **Average Time** | 47 min | 28 min | -19 min |
| **Error Rate** | 68% | 41% | -27 pts |
| **Support Calls** | 890/mo | 412/mo | -54% |
| **Offline Fallback** | 18% | 7% | -11 pts |

You present to the Minister:

You: "The actionable metrics approach worked. By measuring honestly where users struggled, we identified specific problems to fix. Results:

- **Completion rate improved from 70% to 84%** - 14% more users succeed
- **Time reduced from 47 to 28 minutes** - saved 19 minutes per user
- **Support calls dropped 54%** - reduced call center burden
- **Offline fallback down from 18% to 7%** - more users completing digitally

Because completion rate improved, **absolute completions increased 30%** (8,991 → 11,715) even though started registrations only increased 9%. We're helping more people with the same traffic."

Minister: "This is impressive. But what's the lesson? What should we apply across all services?"

You: "The lesson is: **measure outcomes, not just activity.** Here's the framework:"

**ACTIONABLE METRICS FRAMEWORK**

**1. Define Success from User Perspective**
- Not: "How many people visited our website?"
- But: "How many people accomplished what they came to do?"

**2. Measure Completion, Not Just Initiation**  
- Not: "Transactions started"
- But: "Transactions completed successfully"

**3. Track Friction Points**
- Where do users drop off? (funnel analysis)
- Where do errors occur? (error rate by step)
- Where do they need help? (support request patterns)

**4. Measure Time & Effort**
- How long does task take vs how long it should take?
- How many steps vs how many are necessary?

**5. Capture Satisfaction & Sentiment**
- Would users recommend this service?
- How frustrated or satisfied are they?
- Are they better off than before digital option?

**6. Monitor Unintended Consequences**
- Are offline channels increasing (indicating digital failure)?
- Are workarounds emerging (indicating system doesn't meet needs)?
- Are certain user groups left behind?

**7. Use Metrics to Drive Decisions**
- Which problem should we fix first? (biggest drop-off point)
- Did our fix work? (before/after comparison)
- Are we improving over time? (trend analysis)

---

Minister: "I'm convinced. Let's roll this out to all services. But I have a concern - this is more work. Our current dashboard just pulls analytics data. This new approach requires user research, surveys, call center data, field office data. Do we have capacity?"

You: "Valid concern. Here's my proposal:

**Tiered Approach:**

- **Tier 1 (5 highest-volume services)**: Full actionable measurement - completion rates, drop-off analysis, time-on-task, satisfaction surveys, support data integration. These serve 80% of users, so improvement here has biggest impact.

- **Tier 2 (15 medium-volume services)**: Core actionable metrics - completion rate, basic funnel, error tracking. Less intensive than Tier 1 but still actionable.

- **Tier 3 (remaining services)**: Standard metrics plus completion rate. Lighter touch but still measuring outcomes.

We prioritize where impact is greatest, not try to do everything everywhere."

Permanent Secretary: "And what about the political concern - that these metrics might show we're not doing as well as vanity metrics suggest?"

You: "I think we reframe the narrative:

**Old narrative (vanity metrics):**
'We had 1.2 million portal visits and 234,000 transactions. Digital government is succeeding.'

**New narrative (actionable metrics):**
'We're measuring what matters - whether citizens succeed. We found that only 70% of users were completing transactions. We identified the problems, fixed them, and improved completion to 84%. We saved citizens 19 minutes per transaction. We reduced frustrated support calls by 54%. **We're not just reporting numbers - we're improving real experiences.**'

Which story shows better governance? The first says 'things are fine.' The second says 'we measured honestly, found problems, fixed them, and proved improvement.' The second builds trust."

Minister (nodding): "You're right. Citizens don't care if we have 1.2 million visits. They care if the service worked when they needed it. Let's implement this."

**SIX MONTHS LATER - BROADER IMPACT**

The actionable metrics approach has spread:

**Tax Filing Service:**
- Discovered 40% abandonment rate (vanity metric only showed "transactions started")
- Fixed error handling and payment gateway issues
- Completion rate improved from 60% to 79%
- **Impact: 23,000 additional successful tax filings per month**

**Driving License Renewal:**
- Discovered 25% of users completing online still had to visit office (system didn't integrate with printing contractor)
- Fixed integration
- True end-to-end completion improved from 75% to 94%
- **Impact: 5,000 fewer unnecessary office visits per month**

**National ID Application:**
- Discovered average time was 67 minutes (mostly waiting for document upload)
- Implemented background upload and save-and-resume
- Time reduced from 67 to 22 minutes
- **Impact: Saved 45 minutes per citizen, 18,000 hours saved per month**

**Cultural Shift:**

Service teams now start every improvement meeting with: "What does success look like for the user?" rather than "How do we increase transaction volume?"

Call Center Manager: "We went from being seen as overhead to being seen as insight source. Our data now shapes product roadmap."

Developer: "I used to optimize for technical metrics - response time, uptime. Now I optimize for user metrics - completion rate, time-on-task. It's more satisfying because I see real impact."

**LESSONS ON MEASUREMENT:**

1. **Vanity metrics look good but don't inform action** - portal visits, downloads, transactions started, session duration

2. **Actionable metrics reveal problems and drive improvement** - completion rate, task success, time-on-task, satisfaction

3. **Measure outcomes from user perspective, not just system activity** - did they succeed, not just did they visit

4. **Good metrics can be uncomfortable** - they might reveal you're not doing as well as you thought

5. **Leadership often prefers vanity metrics because they look good** - need to reframe as "looking good vs being good"

6. **Measurement drives behavior** - teams optimize for what you measure, so measure what matters

7. **Before/after comparison proves improvement** - measure, improve, measure again

8. **Prioritize measurement effort where impact is greatest** - don't try to measure everything everywhere

9. **Integrate multiple data sources** - analytics + call center + field offices + user research

10. **Tell the story of improvement, not just the snapshot** - narrative of measuring honestly and fixing problems builds more trust than narrative of "everything is great"
rounds.prompt: How do you balance the political need to show success with the operational need to measure honestly and reveal problems?
evaluationCriteria: **Both/And Thinking**: Do they recognize you can show progress AND measure honestly (not either/or)?
**Framing**: Do they understand how to frame honest measurement as strength, not weakness?
**Evidence of Improvement**: Do they see that showing improvement over time is more compelling than showing only success?
**Trust**: Do they recognize that honesty builds long-term credibility even if uncomfortable short-term?
**Audience Segmentation**: Do they distinguish internal (need honest data) from external (want progress story) but keep both transparent?
**Resistance**: Do they understand why leadership resists honest measurement and how to address that concern?
rounds.coachingNotes: The tension between political pressure (show success) and operational need (measure honestly) is real. But it's false choice. You can do both: [1] **Measure honestly internally**: Teams need real data to improve. [2] **Tell improvement story externally**: Don't just report static 'success' - show trajectory of improvement. 'We measured completion rate at 70%, found the problems, fixed them, now at 84%' is MORE impressive than 'we have many transactions.' [3] **Frame honest measurement as governance strength**: 'We don't just report vanity metrics - we measure what matters and prove improvement.' [4] **Build trust over time**: Short-term, vanity metrics feel safer. Long-term, citizens see through gap between metrics and experience. Honest measurement builds credibility. [5] **Understand resistance**: Leaders resist honest metrics because might reveal problems, which could be used against them. Address this by demonstrating that improvement story is MORE compelling than 'everything is fine' story. The PS's concern was valid - opposition might weaponize low metrics. But counter: if you report vanity metrics while citizens experience poor service, that gap is worse than honest measurement with improvement plan.

keyTakeaways: Vanity metrics look impressive but don't inform decisions - portal visits, downloads, transactions started
Actionable metrics reveal problems and drive improvement - completion rates, task success, time-on-task, user satisfaction
Measure outcomes from user perspective (did they succeed?) not just system activity (did they visit?)
Good measurement can be uncomfortable - it might reveal you're not doing as well as you thought, but that's necessary for improvement
Measurement drives behavior - teams optimize for what you measure, so measure what matters most
Before/after comparison proves improvement - establish baseline, make changes, measure again
Prioritize measurement effort where impact is greatest - full actionable measurement for high-volume services, lighter for others
Frame honest measurement as governance strength - showing improvement trajectory is more compelling than static 'success' claims
Integrate multiple data sources - web analytics, call center, field offices, user research - for complete picture
Balance political need to show progress with operational need for honest data - you can do both through improvement narrative

frameworks.name: Vanity vs Actionable Metrics Test
frameworks.description: For each metric, ask: [1] Does it tell us if users succeeded? (No = vanity), [2] Does it inform what to change? (No = vanity), [3] Could it improve while user experience worsens? (Yes = vanity), [4] Does it measure activity or outcome? (Activity = vanity). If vanity, find actionable alternative.
frameworks.application: 'Portal visits' fails test: doesn't tell us if users succeeded, doesn't inform what to change, could increase while experience worsens (repeat visits due to confusion). Alternative: 'Task success rate' - measures if users accomplished goals.

frameworks.name: User Outcome Measurement Framework
frameworks.description: Measure: [1] Completion - % of users who accomplish their goal, [2] Efficiency - time/effort required vs optimal, [3] Error-free - % of experiences without errors or issues, [4] Satisfaction - would user recommend, [5] Equity - do all user groups succeed equally. Focus on user success, not system activity.
frameworks.application: Business registration: Measured completion rate (70%), time required (47 min vs 15 optimal), error rate (68%), drop-off points (Step 4), satisfaction (support call volume). This revealed where users struggled and what to fix.

frameworks.name: Funnel Analysis for Drop-off Diagnosis
frameworks.description: For multi-step processes: [1] Map all steps, [2] Measure % who proceed from each step to next, [3] Identify biggest drop-offs, [4] Investigate why (user research, error logs), [5] Fix highest-impact drop-off first, [6] Measure again. Find where users get stuck.
frameworks.application: Business registration funnel showed: Step 1→2 (99%), Step 2→3 (95%), Step 3→4 (91%), **Step 4→5 (67%)** ← Big problem. Investigated and found beneficial ownership form was confusing. Fixed it, drop-off reduced to 12%.

frameworks.name: Leading vs Lagging Indicators
frameworks.description: **Leading indicators**: Show impact quickly, predict future performance, enable rapid iteration (error rate, drop-off at specific step, support requests). **Lagging indicators**: Show cumulative impact over time, prove overall success, but slow to change (overall completion rate, satisfaction scores). Use leading for rapid improvement, lagging to prove overall impact.
frameworks.application: After fixing Step 4, saw immediate improvement in leading indicator (drop-off at Step 4: 33%→12% within 2 weeks). Lagging indicator (overall completion rate) improved more slowly (70%→84% over 3 months) as cumulative effect built up.

frameworks.name: Tiered Measurement Approach
frameworks.description: Prioritize measurement effort based on impact: [1] **Tier 1** (highest volume/impact): Full actionable measurement - completion, funnel, satisfaction, time-on-task, integrated data. [2] **Tier 2** (medium): Core metrics - completion rate, basic funnel, errors. [3] **Tier 3** (lower volume): Completion rate + standard analytics. Don't try to do everything everywhere.
frameworks.application: Rwanda decided: 5 highest-volume services get full treatment (business registration, tax filing, etc.), 15 medium services get core metrics, remaining get lighter touch. Focus resources where 80% of users are.
